newsitem.title: USA: American Airline pilots set demands, warn of strike.
newsitem.headline: American Airline pilots set demands, warn of strike.

text.p: American Airlines pilots met on Thursday to draw up new labor demands and warned of possible strike action if the carrier refuses to sweeten a contract deal rejected by union members this week.

The 18-member board of directors of the Allied Pilots Association began drawing up the list of demands at a Fort Worth hotel and said they would on Friday define strategy for the next round of talks with the airline's management.

In a surprise vote announced on Wednesday, more than 60 percent of APA members voted against a tentative labor pact with the airline which would have given them a 3 percent wage increase this year and an additional 2 percent in 1999.
"The pilots overwhelmingly said they want several changes to the contract, or we will strike," pilot spokesman Wally Pitts said on Thursday.
The union's five-member negotiating board, which struck the deal rejected by rank-and-file members, stepped down and a replacement board was being named.
The APA's rejection of a labor contract agreed last September after two years of tortuous negotiations effectively put American Airlines' growth plans on hold.

The airline, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., last November pledged to buy 103 jets from Boeing Co. and take out options on 527 more in one of the biggest commercial airplane orders in history.

But Chief Executive Officer Robert Crandall has said the Boeing deal, which at list prices was worth about $6.5 billion and potentially as much as $35 billion, would only go through if pilots ratified a new labor contract.

APA spokesman Gregg Overman said the union would thrash out its new demands by the end of the two-day board of directors meeting on Friday and said that strike action was a possibility, but by no means certain at this stage.
"The rejection of the contract makes the prospect of a strike more real, but a lot of things have to happen before that," Overman said.
The National Mediation Board, which brokered the tentative agreement, now has to decide whether to offer both sides unconditional talks or declare an impasse and offer binding arbitration.
The APA has already made clear it would not accept binding arbitration. If either side refuses the offer, an obligatory 30-day "cooling-off" period would begin.
At the end of the 30 days, the APA would be free to start strike action while American Airlines could either declare a lockout or unilaterally implement new pay and work rules.

Pilots rejected the tentative agreement primarily because of a clause that would have allowed the airline to buy regional jets for its commuter carrier American Eagle, which currently operates only turboprop aircraft.
In return for that concession, American Airlines initially agreed to drop plans to set up a low-fare short-haul unit in which pilots would have taken a pay cut of up to 30 percent.
